atoms.text: The gift that shames: a host gives away or destroys wealth to demonstrate status, so generosity is a form of dominance.
The rival who must reciprocate: a guest is obligated to answer a gift with a larger one, so hospitality escalates into competition.
The destruction of property: valuables are burned or thrown away to prove they are not needed, so waste is a claim to power.
The feast as government: the gathering settles rights to land and resources, so a party is also a parliament.
The outlawed ceremony: the state criminalizes the practice, so a gift economy becomes a crime.
The underground potlatch: the ritual continues in secret despite jail sentences, so tradition survives as resistance.
The oral history recited: the host narrates ancestors and claims, so memory is the title deed.
The winter gathering: wealth accumulated in summer is redistributed in winter, so the year has a built-in reckoning.
The chief who gives everything away: a leader's authority depends on generosity, so power is maintained by loss.
The guest who records a debt: every gift creates an obligation, so the ledger is social rather than financial.
The anthropologist's gaze: outsiders study and misinterpret the ceremony, so the story can stage the theft of meaning.
The democratic inheritance: a nation roots its governance in potlatch law, so an ancient ritual becomes a constitution.
The supernatural guest: the ceremony honors spirits and ancestors, so the dead are participants in the economy.
The potlatch that ruins the host: a leader gives beyond his means and loses everything, so status-seeking is self-destructive.
The gift that cannot be refused: a rival is forced to accept and then cannot repay, so the trap is courtesy.
The revival: a banned ceremony returns after decriminalization, so the story asks what was preserved underground.
